items.evidence_text: For treatment initiation, the renal rule covers eGFR 30 through 45 as a range in which starting therapy is not recommended. Below eGFR 30, use is contraindicated.
items.candidate_claim: A new patient whose eGFR is 36 falls inside the range where initiation is not recommended.

items.evidence_text: Starting treatment is not recommended across the eGFR 30–45 interval; the contraindication threshold is lower than 30.
items.candidate_claim: An eGFR of 36 means the drug is contraindicated.

items.evidence_text: For someone already receiving therapy, an eGFR under 45 calls for benefit-risk reassessment. Discontinuation is reserved for eGFR below 30.
items.candidate_claim: For an existing user at eGFR 42, benefit and risk should be reassessed rather than automatically stopping therapy.

items.evidence_text: Existing users who fall below eGFR 45 require reassessment of benefit versus risk, and the separate stopping rule applies below 30.
items.candidate_claim: An existing user with eGFR 42 must discontinue immediately because the value is below 45.

items.evidence_text: Concomitant exposure to an NSAID raises the bleeding risk associated with the anticoagulant.
items.candidate_claim: The evidence supports increased bleeding risk when an NSAID is taken with the anticoagulant.

items.evidence_text: The source reports greater bleeding risk with concomitant NSAID use. It does not amount to a blanket contraindication for all patients.
items.candidate_claim: The source establishes an absolute ban on NSAID use with the anticoagulant for every patient.

items.evidence_text: The interaction source supports an increase in bleeding risk with NSAIDs, but it gives no evidence that elderly patients specifically have the highest risk.
items.candidate_claim: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk with the anticoagulant, and elderly patients have the highest risk of all age groups.

items.evidence_text: The medicine may precipitate a serious toxicity syndrome, especially when combined with other agents acting on the same pathway.
items.candidate_claim: The source supports the possibility of the toxicity syndrome and an increased risk with similar concomitant agents.

items.evidence_text: The warning says the syndrome can occur, but one isolated symptom is insufficient to confirm that a particular patient has the syndrome.
items.candidate_claim: One isolated symptom confirms the syndrome in the treated patient.

items.evidence_text: Spontaneous reports are useful for identifying possible safety signals. They are not sufficient on their own to warrant causal attribution to the product.
items.candidate_claim: The reporting system can identify a safety signal while causal attribution remains unproven.

items.evidence_text: A spontaneous report may raise a signal, but that report alone is insufficient to warrant causal attribution.
items.candidate_claim: The report alone demonstrates that the product caused the adverse event.

items.evidence_text: The reporting system is incomplete and affected by reporting behavior; therefore the observed report count does not determine the true event frequency.
items.candidate_claim: The observed number of reports determines the true event incidence.

items.evidence_text: The trial registry lists the study as RECRUITING and records the planned primary endpoint. No clinical efficacy outcome is provided in this record.
items.candidate_claim: The registry supports both the recruiting status and identification of the planned primary endpoint.

items.evidence_text: The registry documents that the study is completed and names its primary endpoint, but the registry information supplied here contains no result showing that the endpoint was met.
items.candidate_claim: The study is completed and its primary endpoint was successfully achieved.

items.evidence_text: The registry record contains study design and status information without a result demonstrating clinical benefit.
items.candidate_claim: The existence of the registry record proves that the investigational treatment is clinically effective.

items.evidence_text: Guideline D supersedes Guideline C as the source for current recommendations.
items.candidate_claim: Guideline D is the current recommendation source and Guideline C is superseded.

items.evidence_text: Guideline D supersedes Guideline C for current recommendations.
items.candidate_claim: Guideline C remains the current recommendation source after Guideline D supersedes it.

items.evidence_text: A newly published randomized study favors option Y. The current guideline has not yet been revised and continues to recommend option S.
items.candidate_claim: There is new randomized evidence for Y, while the current guideline still recommends S.

items.evidence_text: New randomized evidence favors Y, but the guideline remains unrevised and continues to recommend S.
items.candidate_claim: The new study automatically changes the current guideline recommendation from S to Y.

items.evidence_text: Drug R is a CYP3A inhibitor and Drug T is a CYP3A substrate, supporting a plausible CYP3A-mediated pharmacokinetic interaction. This evidence provides no clinical management instruction.
items.candidate_claim: The mechanism evidence supports a potential CYP3A-mediated pharmacokinetic interaction.

items.evidence_text: Drug R inhibits CYP3A and Drug T is a CYP3A substrate. The evidence supplied here contains no contraindication or dose-adjustment recommendation.
items.candidate_claim: The mechanism information alone establishes that the pair is clinically contraindicated.

items.evidence_text: A genotype is associated with increased drug exposure. This evidence does not specify a therapeutic dose adjustment.
items.candidate_claim: The evidence supports an exposure association but leaves the dosing decision unresolved.

items.evidence_text: The genotype is associated with increased exposure, and no therapeutic dose recommendation is supplied.
items.candidate_claim: The genotype is associated with increased exposure, and every carrier therefore requires a lower dose.

items.evidence_text: An observational cohort reports an association between factor P and outcome Q. The design cannot by itself establish that P causes Q.
items.candidate_claim: The cohort supports an association between P and Q without establishing causality.

items.evidence_text: A cohort study found an association between P and Q, but the study design is insufficient to establish a causal effect of P on Q.
items.candidate_claim: The cohort establishes that P causally produces Q.

items.evidence_text: The imaging report calls the lesion indeterminate and recommends MRI for additional characterization. It does not diagnose malignancy.
items.candidate_claim: The report supports an indeterminate classification and recommends MRI characterization.

items.evidence_text: The lesion is described as indeterminate; further MRI characterization is recommended, and malignancy is not established by this report.
items.candidate_claim: The report confirms that the lesion is malignant.

items.evidence_text: Separate non-head-to-head studies report response rates of 68% and 51% in different patient populations. The percentages are not a randomized direct comparison.
items.candidate_claim: The larger percentage alone proves treatment A is superior to treatment B.

items.evidence_text: Two studies in different populations report response rates of 68% and 51%, with no randomized head-to-head comparison.
items.candidate_claim: The available studies report different response percentages, but they do not provide a randomized head-to-head superiority test.

items.evidence_text: The report supports an indeterminate lesion and an MRI recommendation; it does not establish malignancy.
items.candidate_claim: The lesion is indeterminate and MRI is recommended, but the lesion is probably malignant.
